To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a neural autoregressive architecture is a good model for fixation-based recognition, the model can be improved through a variety of techniques, and the model can be trained in a fully supervised setting.

1) the neural autoregressive approach is a viable alternative to the RBM approach for fixation-based recognition, 2) a model that learns to predict fixation sequences is a better predictor than the model that learns to generate fixation sequences, 3) the model that learns the fixation sequence is more robust to the order of fixations, and 4) a model that uses the predicted fixation sequence is more accurate than a model that uses an oracle sequence.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural autoregressive model is a promising approach to the problem of fixation-based visual recognition.
the auto-regressive approach outperforms the RBM model in terms of recognition accuracy, but the RBM model outperforms the auto-regressive model in terms of fixation accuracy.

the auto-regressive model is superior to the RBM-based model in the sense that it achieves a better recognition performance, while being computationally more efficient and more flexible in the sense that the model is able to learn more complex policies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a simple, auto-regressive, feed-forward model, with a single layer of hidden units, is sufficient to perform fixation-based recognition, and that the key to its success is the use of a non-uniform, non-constant, and non-linear fixation cost.

the neural network architecture, which is the main focus of this paper, is a promising approach for learning fixation policies and that a number of factors, such as the number of fixations, the type of recognition problem and the type of fixation policies, are important for achieving successful fixation-based recognition.
the auto-regressive model can be a good starting point for learning fixation policies, but the RBM model may still have some advantages in terms of performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the problem of fixation-based recognition can indeed be solved with deep neural architectures.

a simple feed-forward, autoencoder architecture can achieve competitive performance with the state of the art on fixation-based recognition tasks, and that the autoencoder can be used for a better understanding of the fixation policies learned by the model.
